_comment: The committed cgroup limits of the sandboxes.
app_spec.xml, Untrusted Code Sandbox, feature 162:
System rejects a sandboxed run exceeding the cgroup limits for cpu,
memory of 2048 MB or a process count of 32
(docs/nullius-tech-architecture.md section 5.2: the one call site
passes limits=Limits(wall_s=30, cpu_s=30, mem_mb=2048,
network=False, filesystem=False, pids=32), and the control table's
own row is 'Resources | cgroup v2: cpu.max, memory.max, pids.max';
section 3's zone map states the posture the row serves - 'Z1 -
Mutated by the loop | Signal code, exploration policy code | LLM
agents | Sandboxed: no network, no FS, seccomp, cgroup limits').
The compile in packages/sandbox/src/sandbox/budget.py refuses this
file and any change to it that does not declare cpu_s = 30,
mem_mb = 2048 and pids = 32 - so the three numbers below are not a
convention the next edit can forget: they are the law, checked, and a
run whose measured cpu time, memory peak or process count exceeds one
of them is refused with the code cgroup_budget_exceeded.
Why the three are written down at all, when the runner could default
to them. A cgroup limit is a claim about what untrusted code may
consume, and a claim of that shape has to be reviewable: the same
reason feature 157's isolation policy, feature 167's import allowlist,
feature 164's pinning policy and feature 163's wall budget ship as
files rather than as literals in a launcher. The numbers here are the
ones section 5.2's call site passes and the feature's own sentence
names, and the compiler refuses any others - so 'this deployment
confines a run to one core for thirty seconds of cpu, two gigabytes
of memory and thirty-two processes' is a fact about a file in the
repository rather than a line in a runbook.
wall_s is deliberately absent: it is the same Limits(...) call's
first field and it belongs to feature 163's wall-clock law, which
holds it in timeout_policy.json beside its own kill. network and
filesystem are absent for a different reason - they are not budgets
at all but structural denials (section 5.2: 'a namespace with no
interfaces', 'no mounts'), and a boolean that is always False is a
knob nobody turns. This file holds the three fields feature 162's
sentence is about, and each is enforced by one of the cgroup v2
files that sentence's own words name: cpu.max, memory.max, pids.max.
Why 'runner_mem_mb' is here beside 'mem_mb', and why the two differ.
mem_mb is the deployment's cgroup limit - section 5.2's 2048, the
number feature 162's sentence names, the number a breach is measured
against. runner_mem_mb is the host runner's portable RLIMIT_AS
fallback, 4096, and it is larger for a reason that has nothing to do
with a wider budget: jemalloc's address-space reservation for the
interpreter and polars exceeds 2 GiB even at ~70 MB resident, so a
2 GiB RLIMIT_AS is flaky - the child dies before it can run the
signal (evaluator._sandbox.DEFAULT_MEM_MB states this in its own
comment). Both are true and they are different facts about different
mechanisms, so the artifact records both and the compiler refuses
either drifting. A reader who 'reconciles' them by editing one number
would either widen a cgroup past section 5.2 or break every signal
that imports polars; the compile refuses both edits and says so.
pids is the process count of the RUN's own cgroup, which is what
makes an agent-authored signal's exponential forking a contained
event. It is deliberately not section 12's eight-task executor bound:
that one bounds a node's probes for the opposite reason (a node's
work must not collide with another node's) and lives on the executor
plane rather than inside the box. Both numbers are 32 and 8 in the
same document, and a reader who conflated them would file a bug
against a correct deployment.
